quest_011_00.story:
At the edge of sunlit sanctuary courts, Shen Xuan waits until the last lantern is lit before speaking. Shen Xuan is known as a crane rider, but that title has become a shelter for a different kind of work. Tonight Shen Xuan has brought the jade examination tile, wrapped in cloth that smells of rain. Its marks connect a village burned under a false imperial order to the curse spreading through Dawn Sanctuary. Shen Xuan asks Lin Yue to examine the evidence before deciding whom to blame.

The first mark is a narrow cut across the relic's underside. Shen Xuan explains that official records call it damage, while local witnesses call it a signature. A person trying to hide a name would cut deeper; a person trying to preserve one would cut exactly this far. The distinction matters in Dawn Sanctuary, where a refuge that must decide whom forgiveness includes. Lin Yue turns the object toward the light and sees that someone has repaired it more than once.

Su Lian remembers the night differently. Su Lian heard a bell before the storm and a second bell after the soldiers departed. Between those sounds, the courtyard filled with people carrying sealed letters. None were allowed to read what they delivered. The dawn assembly later claimed that every messenger had volunteered. Shen Xuan wants their consent investigated, because a promise made under threat cannot become a sacred oath merely by surviving long enough to be written down.

This chapter is called A Name in Water. Its immediate task is speak with Shen Xuan. That is a practical beginning rather than a complete answer: the mountain cannot be cured by a single sword stroke, and a village cannot be reconciled by declaring one witness pure. Lin Yue agrees to return with a result that can be checked. Shen Xuan insists that neither impressive qi nor an imperial title will substitute for evidence gathered in the living world.

The road to Cloudrest follows an old route used by patients, refugees, and tax collectors. Its stones carry shallow footprints that rain has not erased. Shen Xuan gives Lin Yue a simple rule for the journey: stop whenever a voice offers certainty without a cost. Spirits on this road repeat bargains they barely understood when they were alive. Their answers are useful only when compared with the ordinary details their promises leave behind.

By the roadside, Lin Yue finds a small offering bowl. Someone has placed fresh water beside an old piece of charcoal, a gesture that seems contradictory until Su Lian explains it. The water is for those who survived; the charcoal is for those whose names were burned. Both offerings belong at the same table. Removing one to make the shrine look harmonious would repeat the choice that damaged Dawn Sanctuary in the first place.

The creature called Amber Tiger appears in three different accounts of the disaster. Soldiers described it as a punishment, merchants as a profitable omen, and children as something that stood between them and the fire. Its behavior now follows the pattern of leech. The pattern gives Lin Yue a tactical warning, but it also suggests that the creature remembers a command. A monster can become dangerous while carrying a duty that nobody has released.

Shen Xuan once trusted the dawn assembly because its members promised to protect people without demanding that they become useful first. That promise was tested when food ran short. The council began measuring every household by its ability to repay aid. Those who could not repay were called disloyal. The relic passed through this accounting system and came back with one mark missing. Lin Yue must decide whether the missing mark is an accident or a deliberate erasure.

At an abandoned rest station, a caretaker keeps two copies of the same testimony. One is clean enough for an archive; the other contains corrections made by the people who were present. The clean copy is easier to read and wrong in six important places. Su Lian asks Lin Yue to take both. Destroying the polished lie might satisfy anger, but preserving the comparison gives future readers a way to recognize the method of the deception.

The next clue concerns a village burned under a false imperial order. Shen Xuan has told this part of their history so often that listeners mistake its careful wording for detachment. Shen Xuan chooses each word because careless listeners have used their grief as permission to punish strangers. Lin Yue lets the account remain unfinished. A witness does not owe an audience a satisfying conclusion before her evidence can be believed, and the absence of a neat ending does not make the loss less real.

The relic's qi changes near sunlit sanctuary courts. It does not become stronger; it becomes more specific. A loose vibration resolves into the rhythm of a familiar working song. Shen Xuan recognizes the song because they learned it before they learned to cultivate. Its final verse names a place the official map omits. Lin Yue records the verse instead of immediately following it. A map can be incomplete without every omission being a trap, but this omission has acquired too many guards.

When Lin Yue considers the fighting ahead, she remembers Master Shen's distinction between power and cultivation. Power can interrupt an enemy's body. Cultivation should also interrupt the habit of treating interruption as an answer. Against Amber Tiger, that means observing the warning motion before committing to a strike, keeping a route back to the lanterns, and leaving enough stamina to withdraw. A victory that strands the witness beside a new danger would fail the purpose of the chapter.

Su Lian proposes an easy solution: give the relic to the strongest sect and let its authority settle the dispute. Shen Xuan refuses without accusing the witness of cowardice. Easy solutions become attractive when every difficult solution has already charged a person too much. The refusal therefore needs an alternative. Lin Yue offers to separate the immediate threat from the long argument, so that nobody has to remain in danger merely to preserve the appearance of patience.

That alternative requires attention to ordinary supplies. Moonlotus is gathered because roots hold a memory of clean water; jade essence is studied because its vibration can distinguish a binding from a natural current. Neither material is miraculous by itself. Shen Xuan teaches Lin Yue to describe what was collected, where it was found, and what changed after contact. The lesson makes a record useful to people who do not share the cultivator's instincts or her access to rare techniques.

A messenger from Cloudrest arrives with a request to postpone the work. The request is polite, detailed, and unsigned. Its language praises freedom without abandonment while asking everyone affected by the curse to wait in silence. Lin Yue notices that no date is offered for a new hearing. Su Lian has learned to fear indefinite patience more than open threats. They agree to continue the practical task while keeping the message as another piece of evidence.

During a quiet interval, Shen Xuan speaks about the life she wanted before the disaster. They wanted time to practice their trade well enough that nobody would remember them as extraordinary. The mountain's crisis has turned every useful act into a test of allegiance. Lin Yue understands the exhaustion in that change. A just ending should give people permission to return to ordinary ambitions, rather than replacing one eternal duty with another whose keeper merely has a kinder face.

The danger returns when Amber Tiger senses movement near the old boundary. Its first approach is a warning, its second a commitment. Lin Yue must meet the actual threat rather than the reputation built around it. She watches its distance, keeps the witnesses outside the line of attack, and uses the terrain to break pursuit. The task of speak with Shen Xuan cannot be completed by claiming a kill or a delivery that the world has not actually registered.

After the immediate work, Su Lian asks what should happen to the people who benefited from the lie. Shen Xuan gives a difficult answer: protection should end where it becomes immunity, but blame should stop where the evidence stops. Lin Yue can favor restitution without promising that everyone will be forgiven. She can favor judgment without declaring that the descendants of an offender inherit the offense. The chapter leaves room for both courage and limits.

The jade examination tile now carries enough context to be read as more than a treasure. Its value lies in the relationships it documents: who asked for aid, who supplied it, who altered the terms, and who paid after the agreement was changed. Shen Xuan wants a copy placed somewhere ordinary people can reach. An archive behind a sect's locked gate might preserve the truth while returning ownership of it to the institution that first concealed it.

Lin Yue returns through sunlit sanctuary courts with the result of speak with Shen Xuan. The lantern keeper does not ask how dramatic the journey became. She asks whether the expected evidence arrived and whether anyone must still be searched for. That question sets the measure of success. Shen Xuan records the chapter beside the earlier ones, so that later choices will be judged against the whole sequence rather than the most flattering moment in the cultivator's account.

Before the next chapter begins, Shen Xuan offers a conversation rather than another command. Shen Xuan asks Lin Yue whether freedom without abandonment can survive when it ceases to look heroic. They compare the answer with the fate of Immortal Xu, whose wish to protect his daughter became a binding on an entire mountain. Neither woman treats his grief as a crime. They examine the moment when he decided that grief granted him ownership of someone else's future.

The closing note is deliberately provisional. In Dawn Sanctuary, the immediate task has a measurable result, but the meaning of that result belongs to more than one person. Su Lian receives a copy, Shen Xuan retains another, and Lin Yue carries the route onward. At the end of the twelve-chapter arc, she will choose whether to release the relic's binding or keep its strength. Until then, the work is to make that choice informed rather than inevitable.

The creature has a particular history: The amber in its eyes preserves the torchlight of a hunting party that mistook a healer for a witch.
quest_011_00.mercy: Shen Xuan records the result of the task to speak with Shen Xuan. The account is witnessed rather than final: Su Lian receives a copy, and the next chapter follows the evidence carried by the jade examination tile. The binding's final fate remains undecided.

At the edge of sunlit sanctuary courts, Bai Suyin waits until the last lantern is lit before speaking. Bai Suyin is known as a refuge keeper, but that title has become a shelter for a different kind of work. Tonight Bai Suyin has brought the scarlet mourning ribbon, wrapped in cloth that smells of rain. Its marks connect an apprentice trapped inside an unfinished ritual to the curse spreading through Dawn Sanctuary. Bai Suyin asks Lin Yue to examine the evidence before deciding whom to blame.

The first mark is a narrow cut across the relic's underside. Bai Suyin explains that official records call it damage, while local witnesses call it a signature. A person trying to hide a name would cut deeper; a person trying to preserve one would cut exactly this far. The distinction matters in Dawn Sanctuary, where a refuge that must decide whom forgiveness includes. Lin Yue turns the object toward the light and sees that someone has repaired it more than once.

Zhao Ning remembers the night differently. Zhao Ning heard a bell before the storm and a second bell after the soldiers departed. Between those sounds, the courtyard filled with people carrying sealed letters. None were allowed to read what they delivered. The dawn assembly later claimed that every messenger had volunteered. Bai Suyin wants their consent investigated, because a promise made under threat cannot become a sacred oath merely by surviving long enough to be written down.

This chapter is called The Road of Missing Bells. Its immediate task is visit Lantern Harbor and observe its meridian. That is a practical beginning rather than a complete answer: the mountain cannot be cured by a single sword stroke, and a village cannot be reconciled by declaring one witness pure. Lin Yue agrees to return with a result that can be checked. Bai Suyin insists that neither impressive qi nor an imperial title will substitute for evidence gathered in the living world.

The road to Lantern Harbor follows an old route used by patients, refugees, and tax collectors. Its stones carry shallow footprints that rain has not erased. Bai Suyin gives Lin Yue a simple rule for the journey: stop whenever a voice offers certainty without a cost. Spirits on this road repeat bargains they barely understood when they were alive. Their answers are useful only when compared with the ordinary details their promises leave behind.

By the roadside, Lin Yue finds a small offering bowl. Someone has placed fresh water beside an old piece of charcoal, a gesture that seems contradictory until Zhao Ning explains it. The water is for those who survived; the charcoal is for those whose names were burned. Both offerings belong at the same table. Removing one to make the shrine look harmonious would repeat the choice that damaged Dawn Sanctuary in the first place.

The creature called Jade Frog appears in three different accounts of the disaster. Soldiers described it as a punishment, merchants as a profitable omen, and children as something that stood between them and the fire. Its behavior now follows the pattern of leech. The pattern gives Lin Yue a tactical warning, but it also suggests that the creature remembers a command. A monster can become dangerous while carrying a duty that nobody has released.

Bai Suyin once trusted the dawn assembly because its members promised to protect people without demanding that they become useful first. That promise was tested when food ran short. The council began measuring every household by its ability to repay aid. Those who could not repay were called disloyal. The relic passed through this accounting system and came back with one mark missing. Lin Yue must decide whether the missing mark is an accident or a deliberate erasure.

At an abandoned rest station, a caretaker keeps two copies of the same testimony. One is clean enough for an archive; the other contains corrections made by the people who were present. The clean copy is easier to read and wrong in six important places. Zhao Ning asks Lin Yue to take both. Destroying the polished lie might satisfy anger, but preserving the comparison gives future readers a way to recognize the method of the deception.

The next clue concerns an apprentice trapped inside an unfinished ritual. Bai Suyin has told this part of their history so often that listeners mistake its careful wording for detachment. Bai Suyin chooses each word because careless listeners have used their grief as permission to punish strangers. Lin Yue lets the account remain unfinished. A witness does not owe an audience a satisfying conclusion before her evidence can be believed, and the absence of a neat ending does not make the loss less real.

The relic's qi changes near sunlit sanctuary courts. It does not become stronger; it becomes more specific. A loose vibration resolves into the rhythm of a familiar working song. Bai Suyin recognizes the song because they learned it before they learned to cultivate. Its final verse names a place the official map omits. Lin Yue records the verse instead of immediately following it. A map can be incomplete without every omission being a trap, but this omission has acquired too many guards.

When Lin Yue considers the fighting ahead, she remembers Master Shen's distinction between power and cultivation. Power can interrupt an enemy's body. Cultivation should also interrupt the habit of treating interruption as an answer. Against Jade Frog, that means observing the warning motion before committing to a strike, keeping a route back to the lanterns, and leaving enough stamina to withdraw. A victory that strands the witness beside a new danger would fail the purpose of the chapter.

Zhao Ning proposes an easy solution: give the relic to the strongest sect and let its authority settle the dispute. Bai Suyin refuses without accusing the witness of cowardice. Easy solutions become attractive when every difficult solution has already charged a person too much. The refusal therefore needs an alternative. Lin Yue offers to separate the immediate threat from the long argument, so that nobody has to remain in danger merely to preserve the appearance of patience.

That alternative requires attention to ordinary supplies. Moonlotus is gathered because roots hold a memory of clean water; jade essence is studied because its vibration can distinguish a binding from a natural current. Neither material is miraculous by itself. Bai Suyin teaches Lin Yue to describe what was collected, where it was found, and what changed after contact. The lesson makes a record useful to people who do not share the cultivator's instincts or her access to rare techniques.

A messenger from Lantern Harbor arrives with a request to postpone the work. The request is polite, detailed, and unsigned. Its language praises memory without imprisonment while asking everyone affected by the curse to wait in silence. Lin Yue notices that no date is offered for a new hearing. Zhao Ning has learned to fear indefinite patience more than open threats. They agree to continue the practical task while keeping the message as another piece of evidence.

During a quiet interval, Bai Suyin speaks about the life she wanted before the disaster. They wanted time to practice their trade well enough that nobody would remember them as extraordinary. The mountain's crisis has turned every useful act into a test of allegiance. Lin Yue understands the exhaustion in that change. A just ending should give people permission to return to ordinary ambitions, rather than replacing one eternal duty with another whose keeper merely has a kinder face.

The danger returns when Jade Frog senses movement near the old boundary. Its first approach is a warning, its second a commitment. Lin Yue must meet the actual threat rather than the reputation built around it. She watches its distance, keeps the witnesses outside the line of attack, and uses the terrain to break pursuit. The task of visit Lantern Harbor and observe its meridian cannot be completed by claiming a kill or a delivery that the world has not actually registered.

After the immediate work, Zhao Ning asks what should happen to the people who benefited from the lie. Bai Suyin gives a difficult answer: protection should end where it becomes immunity, but blame should stop where the evidence stops. Lin Yue can favor restitution without promising that everyone will be forgiven. She can favor judgment without declaring that the descendants of an offender inherit the offense. The chapter leaves room for both courage and limits.

The scarlet mourning ribbon now carries enough context to be read as more than a treasure. Its value lies in the relationships it documents: who asked for aid, who supplied it, who altered the terms, and who paid after the agreement was changed. Bai Suyin wants a copy placed somewhere ordinary people can reach. An archive behind a sect's locked gate might preserve the truth while returning ownership of it to the institution that first concealed it.

Lin Yue returns through sunlit sanctuary courts with the result of visit Lantern Harbor and observe its meridian. The lantern keeper does not ask how dramatic the journey became. She asks whether the expected evidence arrived and whether anyone must still be searched for. That question sets the measure of success. Bai Suyin records the chapter beside the earlier ones, so that later choices will be judged against the whole sequence rather than the most flattering moment in the cultivator's account.

Before the next chapter begins, Bai Suyin offers a conversation rather than another command. Bai Suyin asks Lin Yue whether memory without imprisonment can survive when it ceases to look heroic. They compare the answer with the fate of Immortal Xu, whose wish to protect his daughter became a binding on an entire mountain. Neither woman treats his grief as a crime. They examine the moment when he decided that grief granted him ownership of someone else's future.

The closing note is deliberately provisional. In Dawn Sanctuary, the immediate task has a measurable result, but the meaning of that result belongs to more than one person. Zhao Ning receives a copy, Bai Suyin retains another, and Lin Yue carries the route onward. At the end of the twelve-chapter arc, she will choose whether to release the relic's binding or keep its strength. Until then, the work is to make that choice informed rather than inevitable.

The creature has a particular history: Its croak repeats the password of a refuge that admitted soldiers after promising to shelter their victims.

At the edge of sunlit sanctuary courts, Zhao Hua waits until the last lantern is lit before speaking. Zhao Hua is known as a river mediator, but that title has become a shelter for a different kind of work. Tonight Zhao Hua has brought the ink-stained name slip, wrapped in cloth that smells of rain. Its marks connect a daughter whose dreams were confiscated as tax to the curse spreading through Dawn Sanctuary. Zhao Hua asks Lin Yue to examine the evidence before deciding whom to blame.

The first mark is a narrow cut across the relic's underside. Zhao Hua explains that official records call it damage, while local witnesses call it a signature. A person trying to hide a name would cut deeper; a person trying to preserve one would cut exactly this far. The distinction matters in Dawn Sanctuary, where a refuge that must decide whom forgiveness includes. Lin Yue turns the object toward the light and sees that someone has repaired it more than once.

Mei Lan remembers the night differently. Mei Lan heard a bell before the storm and a second bell after the soldiers departed. Between those sounds, the courtyard filled with people carrying sealed letters. None were allowed to read what they delivered. The dawn assembly later claimed that every messenger had volunteered. Zhao Hua wants their consent investigated, because a promise made under threat cannot become a sacred oath merely by surviving long enough to be written down.

This chapter is called A Witness Who Remembers. Its immediate task is speak with Mei Lan. That is a practical beginning rather than a complete answer: the mountain cannot be cured by a single sword stroke, and a village cannot be reconciled by declaring one witness pure. Lin Yue agrees to return with a result that can be checked. Zhao Hua insists that neither impressive qi nor an imperial title will substitute for evidence gathered in the living world.

The road to Whispering Reed follows an old route used by patients, refugees, and tax collectors. Its stones carry shallow footprints that rain has not erased. Zhao Hua gives Lin Yue a simple rule for the journey: stop whenever a voice offers certainty without a cost. Spirits on this road repeat bargains they barely understood when they were alive. Their answers are useful only when compared with the ordinary details their promises leave behind.

By the roadside, Lin Yue finds a small offering bowl. Someone has placed fresh water beside an old piece of charcoal, a gesture that seems contradictory until Mei Lan explains it. The water is for those who survived; the charcoal is for those whose names were burned. Both offerings belong at the same table. Removing one to make the shrine look harmonious would repeat the choice that damaged Dawn Sanctuary in the first place.

The creature called Basalt Yak appears in three different accounts of the disaster. Soldiers described it as a punishment, merchants as a profitable omen, and children as something that stood between them and the fire. Its behavior now follows the pattern of leech. The pattern gives Lin Yue a tactical warning, but it also suggests that the creature remembers a command. A monster can become dangerous while carrying a duty that nobody has released.

Zhao Hua once trusted the dawn assembly because its members promised to protect people without demanding that they become useful first. That promise was tested when food ran short. The council began measuring every household by its ability to repay aid. Those who could not repay were called disloyal. The relic passed through this accounting system and came back with one mark missing. Lin Yue must decide whether the missing mark is an accident or a deliberate erasure.

At an abandoned rest station, a caretaker keeps two copies of the same testimony. One is clean enough for an archive; the other contains corrections made by the people who were present. The clean copy is easier to read and wrong in six important places. Mei Lan asks Lin Yue to take both. Destroying the polished lie might satisfy anger, but preserving the comparison gives future readers a way to recognize the method of the deception.

The next clue concerns a daughter whose dreams were confiscated as tax. Zhao Hua has told this part of their history so often that listeners mistake its careful wording for detachment. Zhao Hua chooses each word because careless listeners have used their grief as permission to punish strangers. Lin Yue lets the account remain unfinished. A witness does not owe an audience a satisfying conclusion before her evidence can be believed, and the absence of a neat ending does not make the loss less real.

The relic's qi changes near sunlit sanctuary courts. It does not become stronger; it becomes more specific. A loose vibration resolves into the rhythm of a familiar working song. Zhao Hua recognizes the song because they learned it before they learned to cultivate. Its final verse names a place the official map omits. Lin Yue records the verse instead of immediately following it. A map can be incomplete without every omission being a trap, but this omission has acquired too many guards.

When Lin Yue considers the fighting ahead, she remembers Master Shen's distinction between power and cultivation. Power can interrupt an enemy's body. Cultivation should also interrupt the habit of treating interruption as an answer. Against Basalt Yak, that means observing the warning motion before committing to a strike, keeping a route back to the lanterns, and leaving enough stamina to withdraw. A victory that strands the witness beside a new danger would fail the purpose of the chapter.

Mei Lan proposes an easy solution: give the relic to the strongest sect and let its authority settle the dispute. Zhao Hua refuses without accusing the witness of cowardice. Easy solutions become attractive when every difficult solution has already charged a person too much. The refusal therefore needs an alternative. Lin Yue offers to separate the immediate threat from the long argument, so that nobody has to remain in danger merely to preserve the appearance of patience.

That alternative requires attention to ordinary supplies. Moonlotus is gathered because roots hold a memory of clean water; jade essence is studied because its vibration can distinguish a binding from a natural current. Neither material is miraculous by itself. Zhao Hua teaches Lin Yue to describe what was collected, where it was found, and what changed after contact. The lesson makes a record useful to people who do not share the cultivator's instincts or her access to rare techniques.

A messenger from Whispering Reed arrives with a request to postpone the work. The request is polite, detailed, and unsigned. Its language praises memory without imprisonment while asking everyone affected by the curse to wait in silence. Lin Yue notices that no date is offered for a new hearing. Mei Lan has learned to fear indefinite patience more than open threats. They agree to continue the practical task while keeping the message as another piece of evidence.

During a quiet interval, Zhao Hua speaks about the life she wanted before the disaster. They wanted time to practice their trade well enough that nobody would remember them as extraordinary. The mountain's crisis has turned every useful act into a test of allegiance. Lin Yue understands the exhaustion in that change. A just ending should give people permission to return to ordinary ambitions, rather than replacing one eternal duty with another whose keeper merely has a kinder face.

The danger returns when Basalt Yak senses movement near the old boundary. Its first approach is a warning, its second a commitment. Lin Yue must meet the actual threat rather than the reputation built around it. She watches its distance, keeps the witnesses outside the line of attack, and uses the terrain to break pursuit. The task of speak with Mei Lan cannot be completed by claiming a kill or a delivery that the world has not actually registered.

After the immediate work, Mei Lan asks what should happen to the people who benefited from the lie. Zhao Hua gives a difficult answer: protection should end where it becomes immunity, but blame should stop where the evidence stops. Lin Yue can favor restitution without promising that everyone will be forgiven. She can favor judgment without declaring that the descendants of an offender inherit the offense. The chapter leaves room for both courage and limits.

The ink-stained name slip now carries enough context to be read as more than a treasure. Its value lies in the relationships it documents: who asked for aid, who supplied it, who altered the terms, and who paid after the agreement was changed. Zhao Hua wants a copy placed somewhere ordinary people can reach. An archive behind a sect's locked gate might preserve the truth while returning ownership of it to the institution that first concealed it.

Lin Yue returns through sunlit sanctuary courts with the result of speak with Mei Lan. The lantern keeper does not ask how dramatic the journey became. She asks whether the expected evidence arrived and whether anyone must still be searched for. That question sets the measure of success. Zhao Hua records the chapter beside the earlier ones, so that later choices will be judged against the whole sequence rather than the most flattering moment in the cultivator's account.

Before the next chapter begins, Zhao Hua offers a conversation rather than another command. Zhao Hua asks Lin Yue whether memory without imprisonment can survive when it ceases to look heroic. They compare the answer with the fate of Immortal Xu, whose wish to protect his daughter became a binding on an entire mountain. Neither woman treats his grief as a crime. They examine the moment when he decided that grief granted him ownership of someone else's future.

The closing note is deliberately provisional. In Dawn Sanctuary, the immediate task has a measurable result, but the meaning of that result belongs to more than one person. Mei Lan receives a copy, Zhao Hua retains another, and Lin Yue carries the route onward. At the end of the twelve-chapter arc, she will choose whether to release the relic's binding or keep its strength. Until then, the work is to make that choice informed rather than inevitable.

The creature has a particular history: The yak hauled stone for a workers' memorial that was quietly repurposed into a monument to the forge's owner.
